quote_a: *  Public clients MUST use PKCE [RFC7636] to this end, as motivated in Section 4.5.3.1.
evidence: 6749 predates PKCE and contains no code_challenge/code_verifier requirement, so public clients using only the authorization code grant per 6749 are exposed to authorization code injection and interception attacks that 9700's mandatory PKCE prevents.

quote_a: Authorization servers MUST support PKCE [RFC7636].
evidence: 6749 defines no PKCE support obligation for authorization servers; 9700 makes it a MUST. A 6749-only authorization server cannot serve PKCE clients and leaves public clients without injection defenses.

quote_a: Authorization servers MUST mitigate PKCE downgrade attacks by ensuring that a token request containing a code_verifier parameter is accepted only if a code_challenge parameter was present
evidence: 6749 has no PKCE downgrade notion (no PKCE at all); 9700 requires rejecting code_verifier-bearing token requests whose authorization request lacked a code_challenge. 6749-only servers accepting such requests enable downgrade/interception.

quote_a: MUST prevent mix-up attacks.  Two different methods are discussed below.
evidence: 6749 never addresses mix-up attacks (responses from wrong issuer); 9700 requires clients to store and compare issuer identifiers or use per-issuer redirect URIs. Multi-issuer clients built purely on 6749 can silently accept tokens minted by a hostile authorization server.

quote_a: *  Clients MUST NOT pass access tokens in a URI query parameter in the way described in Section 2.3 of [RFC6750].
evidence: 6749 does not constrain how clients pass tokens to resource servers (deferring to RFC 6750's query option); 9700 forbids URI-query token passing because tokens leak via logs/history/referrers. Clients relying on the query method permitted by 6750/6749 leak tokens.

quote_a: Authorization and resource servers SHOULD use mechanisms for sender-constraining access tokens, such as mutual TLS for OAuth 2.0 [RFC8705] or OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) [RFC9449]
evidence: 6749 treats access tokens as opaque bearer credentials with no sender-constraining concept; 9700 recommends mTLS/DPoP binding so stolen tokens cannot be replayed. 6749-only deployments rely solely on token confidentiality.

quote_a: Clients MUST NOT expose open redirectors.  Attackers may use open redirectors to produce URLs pointing to the client and utilize them to exfiltrate authorization codes and access tokens,
evidence: 6749 never forbids open redirectors on client web servers; 9700 issues a MUST NOT because they enable code/token exfiltration and phishing. 6749-only client implementations may run forwarding endpoints that exfiltrate authorization responses.

quote_a: *  The resource server MUST treat access tokens like other sensitive secrets and not store or transfer them in plaintext.
evidence: 6749 imposes confidentiality/TLS requirements for token transit (Sec 10.3) but no explicit storage/plaintext-handling MUST for resource servers; 9700 adds it. Resource servers persisting tokens in plaintext are compliant with 6749 yet leak tokens on compromise.

quote_a: It is RECOMMENDED to use end-to-end TLS according to [BCP195] between the client and the resource server.
evidence: 6749 requires TLS for token transmission but says nothing about end-to-end (no intermediary TLS termination) client-to-resource-server connections; 9700 recommends BCP195 end-to-end TLS to prevent token interception at intermediaries.

quote_a: The authorization server MUST verify the binding between the refresh token and client identity whenever the client identity can be authenticated.
quote_b: The authorization server MUST verify the binding between the refresh token and client identity whenever the client identity can be authenticated. When client authentication is not possible, the authorization server SHOULD issue sender-constrained refresh tokens or use refresh token rotation
evidence: For unauthenticatable (public) clients, 6749 leaves refresh-abuse detection open ('SHOULD deploy other means', line 3129); 2.1 concretely requires sender-constrained refresh tokens or rotation, changing refresh-token issuance behavior for public clients.

quote_a: The authorization server MUST prevent attackers from guessing access tokens, authorization codes, refresh tokens, resource owner passwords, and client credentials.
quote_b: The authorization server MUST prevent attackers from guessing access tokens, authorization codes, refresh tokens, resource owner passwords, and client credentials.
evidence: Identical guessing-prevention rule in both, but 2.1 sets the probability bound at 2^-128/2^-160 (draft 3731) for values 'not intended for handling by end users' — a sharper conformance target than 6749's phrasing; borderline editorial but yields a testable divergence for credential entropy.

The draft only has a general RECOMMENDED end-to-end-TLS remark and contains no reverse-proxy header-sanitization or inter-hop protection requirements (grep for 'proxy' finds only incidental matches).

Authorization endpoints built to 6749 have no such obligations.

quote_b: value. This specification defines the value code, which must be used to signal that the client wants to use the authorization code flow.
evidence: The entire implicit-grant response section of 6749 (access token returned via front-channel, refresh token MUST NOT be issued) has no counterpart in 2.1 — the flow is removed, so all implicit-grant provisions of 6749 are dropped provisions. Implementations relying on front-channel token delivery must migrate to the authorization code grant.

quote_a: Refresh tokens for public clients MUST be sender-constrained or use refresh token rotation as described in Section 4.14.
quote_b: the authorization server SHOULD issue sender-constrained refresh tokens or use refresh token rotation as described in Section 4.3.1.
evidence: The BCP makes sender-constraint or rotation of public-client refresh tokens a MUST; OAuth 2.1 weakens it to a SHOULD. This is a direct RFC 2119 strength downgrade of a core refresh-token protection, not a rewording.

quote_a: Authorization servers MUST determine, based on a risk assessment, whether to issue refresh tokens to a certain client.
quote_b: Authorization servers SHOULD determine, based on a risk assessment and their own policies, whether to issue refresh tokens to a certain client.
evidence: Same substantive requirement (risk assessment before issuing refresh tokens) downgraded from MUST to SHOULD in OAuth 2.1.

quote_b: MUST prevent mix-up attacks. Two different methods are discussed in the following.
evidence: RFC 9700 Section 4.17.2 carries MUSTs for in-browser (postMessage) OAuth flows: exact string matching of receiver origins (line 2186), no wildcard postMessage targets (line 2199), and client-side injection prevention/exact-origin matching (lines 2204-2205). The draft's corresponding Section 7.15 (lines 4064-4149) reproduces only the two mix-up defenses (iss comparison and distinct redirect URIs); the postMessage-origin requirements are absent from the draft (no 'postMessage' occurrences).

quote_a: Authorization servers SHOULD enforce client authentication if it is feasible, in the particular deployment, to establish a process for issuance/registration of credentials for clients and ensuring the confidentiality of those credentials.
quote_b: The authorization server MUST only rely on client authentication if the process of issuance/registration and distribution of the underlying credentials ensures their confidentiality.
evidence: BCP affirmatively directs servers to enforce client authentication (SHOULD enforce when feasible); the draft instead only conditions reliance on already-performed authentication (MUST only rely if...) plus a softer 'SHOULD employ other means to validate the client's identity' (line 1361). The affirmative enforcement recommendation of RFC 9700 2.5 is not carried forward at the same strength.

quote_a: ensure that the "redirect_uri" parameter is present if the "redirect_uri" parameter was included in the initial authorization request as described in Section 4.1.1, and if included ensure that their values are identical.
quote_b: For backwards compatibility of an authorization server wishing to support both OAuth 2.0 and OAuth 2.1 clients, the authorization server MUST allow clients to send the redirect_uri parameter in the token request (Section 4.1.3), and MUST enforce the parameter as described in [RFC6749].
evidence: OAuth 2.1 removes the redirect_uri parameter from the token request for 2.1 clients (Section 4.1.3 parameter table has no redirect_uri; changelog line 5570 'removed redirect_uri from the token request'), whereas RFC 9700 4.5.2 (via RFC 6749) treats the redirect_uri comparison at the token endpoint as an authorization-code-injection defense that providers are observed to wrongly skip (lines 1242-1244). The draft retains enforcement only as a backwards-compatibility path for OAuth 2.0 clients, i.e., the BCP-recognized injection defense is dropped from the 2.1 flow (PKCE is the substitute, but the BCP check is not carried forward).

quote_a: Therefore, [RFC6749] further recommends that, when an attempt is made to redeem a code twice, the authorization server SHOULD revoke all tokens issued previously based on that code.
quote_b: The authorization server SHOULD NOT revoke any issued tokens when receiving a replayed authorization code that contains invalid parameters.
evidence: Direct tension in the code-replay response: the BCP (following RFC 6749) says the server SHOULD revoke all tokens on a second redemption attempt; the draft adds a carve-out the BCP lacks — SHOULD NOT revoke when the replayed request has invalid parameters (e.g., wrong client auth or verifier), citing a DoS vector (lines 3598-3608). The two documents give opposite-facing SHOULD guidance for overlapping replay scenarios; the draft also conditions revocation on request validity (line 3598), a weakening introduced in 2.1.

quote_a: When using PKCE, clients SHOULD use PKCE code challenge methods that do not expose the PKCE verifier in the authorization request. Otherwise, attackers could maliciously select ...
quote_b: an unverifiable downgrade attack vector, as servers cannot distinguish legitimate constrained clients from attacker-modified requests claiming to be constrained.
evidence: Direction of strictness differs: the BCP leaves the 'plain' method as a SHOULD-avoid (clients SHOULD use non-plaintext challenge methods), while the draft forbids it outright for OAuth 2.1 (code_challenge_method is 'REQUIRED, the value S256 or a value defined by a future extension', line 2068, and Section 7.5.2 deprecates plain). This is a v2-1 requirement stricter than the BCP, not a drop.

quote_a: Authorization servers MUST mitigate PKCE downgrade attacks by ensuring that a token request containing a code_verifier parameter is accepted only if a code_challenge parameter was present in the authorization request.
quote_b: If there was no code_challenge in the authorization request associated with the authorization code in the token request, the authorization server MUST reject the token request.
evidence: Verified consistent (also draft lines 1785, 2303-2304, 3565-3566): the draft not only carries the BCP's PKCE-downgrade mitigation forward but strengthens it — BCP 2.1.1 required rejecting verifier-without-challenge, while the draft additionally rejects token requests for codes with no code_challenge at all except the confidential-client+nonce carve-out of 7.5.1.1. Reported only to record that this focus area is NOT a divergence; no dropped or weakened provision here.
